The active 3D cloak uses a conformal array of radiating sources surrounding a conductive cylindrical target.
The target cylinder has a radius of 101.5 mm and height of 753 mm.
The cloak operates at 1.2 GHz using a ridged horn antenna as the illuminating source.
The cloak array consists of 15 dipole antenna elements arranged in 6 vertical rows with 125.6 mm spacing.
Active cloaking cancels scattered fields by generating a field discontinuity with a 180° phase shift relative to the scattered field.
Simulated bistatic radar cross-section (RCS) shows average scattering suppression of 18.4 dB (individual feeding) and 17 dB (column feeding).
Experimental RCS measurements show average scattering suppression of 7.7 dB (simulation-based weights) and 8.3 dB (experiment-based weights).
Maximum experimental scattering suppression peaks reach 37.5 dB and 34.2 dB respectively.
The cloak elements are fed via a 16-channel controller with voltage-controlled attenuators and phase shifters.
Column feeding simplifies control by feeding elements in the same vertical column with the same input.
Conductive targets short out electric surface currents, allowing cloak design with only magnetic sources.
The cloak was experimentally validated in an anechoic chamber with absorptive foam cones to reduce reflections.
The cloak achieves suppression over an azimuthal range of 30° to 315° around the target.
The experimental setup uses a probe horn mounted on a rotating tripod to measure scattered fields at a fixed radius.
The cloak shows a fractional bandwidth of approximately 13% around 1.2 GHz with 3 dB bandwidths of 6-7%.
Experimental weights derived from real incident field measurements provide better matching than simulation-based weights.
The cloak design is based on extrapolating a previous 2D circular cloak layout into a 3D array.
Full-wave simulations were performed using Ansys HFSS with PML boundary conditions to enforce free-space conditions.
The cloak can accommodate multiple frequencies and polarizations due to its active nature.
The paper demonstrates the first 3D active interior cloak under free-space conditions.
